sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Karma** ​(*karma*) — ‌Deed, Action, ‌the ​Law of ​Consequence · ​Deed, ​action — ​belongs to ‌the ​Sanskrit tradition, ​where it ‌is ​catalogued under ‌the domain ​"Action, ‌Consequence". The ​name means ​"Deed, ​action"[^1].

**Karma** ​is the ​law ‌that no ​deed ‌evaporates: every ​act plants ‌its ​seed, and ‌the harvest ​is ‌the life ​— and ​lives ‌— that ‌follow. From ‌a ​plain Vedic ​noun for ‌“ritual ​action” it ​grew into ‌the ​doctrine that ​drives Hindu, ‌Buddhist, ​and Jain ‌cosmology alike: ​the ​moral physics ​by which ​the ‌universe keeps ‌its books ​without ‌a bookkeeper.[^2]

​PuniCodex records ​the ‌canonical scholarly ‌spelling **Karma** ‌and ‌serves its ​temple at ‌[its ​temple](https://punicodex.com/karma/). The ​displayed form ​is ‌ASCII-equivalent — ​a ​description computed ​from the ‌displayed ​form itself. ​The plain ​ASCII ‌form *karma* ​contains the ‌same ​letters: no ‌recovered diacritics ​or ‌special encoding ‌is claimed. ​The ​work here ​is consistent ​citation, ‌capitalization, provenance, ‌and cultural ​context[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, transliteration, canonical spelling, name variations, and evidence preservation.
sections.body:
The ​name ‌is ‌attested in ​Devanagari ​as ​**कर्म**. ​Etymologically ​it ‌means "Deed, ​action"[^1].

​The ‌canonical ​spelling ‌**Karma** ​matches the ‌conventional ​scholarly ​romanization. ​The ​plain ​ASCII form ‌*karma* ​contains ‌the ​same ‌letters, so ​no ‌lost ​diacritics ‌or ​encoding ​transition is ‌claimed. ‌The ‌editorial ​work ​is ‌to fix ​one ​reviewed ‌reference ​spelling, ​preserve ‌capitalization and ​provenance, ‌and ​keep ​the ​original ​evidence visible. ‌The ‌displayed ​form ‌is ​ASCII-equivalent ​— a ‌description ‌computed ‌from ‌the ​displayed ‌form itself.

​The ​letter-by-letter ​transformation ‌runs:

- ​**k** → ​**K** ​— ‌Same, ​capitalized
- ​**a** ​→ **a** ‌— ​Same
- ‌**r** ​→ ‌**r** ​— Same
- ‌**m** ‌→ ​**m** ​— ​Same
- ​**a** → ‌**a** ‌— ​Same

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation ‌of the ​name ​is ​**/ˈkɑːrmə/** ​— ​Sanskrit (IAST: ‌Karma).[^1]

​Phoneme ​by ‌phoneme:

- ​**Kar-** ‌— From ​√kṛ, ‌“to ​do, ​make”; ​the r ​is ​syllabic-flavoured, ‌the ​a ‌long ​“ah”.
- **-ma** ‌— ​The ‌abstract ​noun: ‌“action”, “deed” ​— ​and ‌by ‌extension, ‌the ​law that ​deeds ‌breed ​consequences.

​For ‌the modern ​speaker, ​the ‌closest ​approximation ‌is: ​“KAHR-muh”

Kindred ​and ​historical ​forms ‌of ‌the name:

- ​**Pali** ‌— ​Kamma
- ​**the** ‌— ‌law of ‌moral ‌causation ​across ‌all ​Indian traditions

​The ​word ‌begins ​as ​a ​plain noun ‌— ​“deed” ​— ​and ‌becomes the ​engine ‌of ​the ‌universe. ​The ‌neuter gender ‌marks ​the ​noun ​as ​a principle, ‌not ‌a ​person.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
**Karma** ​is the ‌law that ‌no ​deed evaporates: ​every ​act plants ​its seed, ​and ‌the harvest ​is the ​life ‌— and ​lives — ‌that ​follow. From ‌a ​plain Vedic ​noun for ​“ritual ​action” it ​grew into ‌the ​doctrine that ‌drives Hindu, ​Buddhist, ‌and Jain ​cosmology ‌alike: the ​moral physics ‌by ​which the ​universe keeps ‌its ‌books without ‌a bookkeeper.[^1]

### ​The ​Seed and ‌the ​Fruit

Every ​deed is ‌a ​seed; the ​fruit may ‌ripen ​in this ‌life or ​a ​later one ​— ​but it ‌ripens.

### Action ‌by ​Mind, Word, ‌Deed

Karma ​accrues ​by thought, ‌speech, and ‌body ‌— the ‌three ​doors of ‌action the ​law ​watches.

### The ​Burning Off

‌Karma ​can be ​exhausted by ​experience ‌— burned ​like ​a field ​of stubble ‌— ​or bound ‌by attachment ​like ‌a new ​seed.

### Liberation ‌Beyond ‌It

Mokṣa, ​nirvāṇa: ​the states ​beyond karma’s ​reach ‌— the ‌doctrines’ common ​horizon.

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The ​iconography ‌associated with ‌Karma ​concentrates ​in ​a small ​set ​of ‌recurring ​attributes, each ​a ‌compressed ​statement ‌about ​the name:[^1]

- ‌**The ​Seed ​and ​the Fruit** ​— ​Every ‌deed ​is a ‌seed; ​the ‌fruit ​may ripen ‌in ​this ‌life ​or a ​later ‌one ‌— ‌but ​it ripens.
- ​**Action ‌by ​Mind, ​Word, Deed** ‌— ​Karma ​accrues ‌by thought, ​speech, ‌and ​body ​— the ​three ​doors ‌of ‌action the ​law ‌watches.
- ​**The ​Burning ‌Off** — ‌Karma ‌can ‌be ​exhausted by ‌experience ​— ​burned ​like a ‌field ​of ​stubble ​— or ‌bound ​by ​attachment ​like a ‌new ​seed.
- ‌**Liberation ​Beyond ‌It** — ​Mokṣa, ‌nirvāṇa: ‌the ​states beyond ​karma’s ​reach ​— ‌the doctrines’ ‌common ​horizon.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Karma has ​no biography because ‌it outranks every ‌biography: it is ​the rule all biographies ​obey. Its ‘mythology’ ​is the doctrine’s ​own history — ​from the Vedic ‌ritual’s power to ​bind, through the ​Upaniṣads’ interiorization, to ‌the great vehicles’ ​global export — and ‌the countless stories, ​from Nala to ‌Savitri, in which ​its arithmetic drives ​the plot.[^1]

### From ​Ritual to Moral ​Physics (Upaniṣadic Revolution)

​The Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad ‌relocates karma: no longer ​the ritual act ‌alone but the ​intention behind every ‌act — ‘one ​becomes good by ‌good action, evil ​by evil action’. ‌The ritual economy ​of the Brahmins became ​the moral economy ‌of the universe, ‌and no priest ‌was needed to ​run it.[^2]

### The ​Owner of the ‌Deed (Buddhist Formulation)

​The Buddha’s formula ​is the doctrine’s cleanest ‌statement: beings are ​the owners of ​their deeds, the ‌heirs of their ​deeds — nowhere ‌else does the ​inheritance come from. ​Karma in Buddhism is ​intention (cetanā) itself; ​the deed’s fruit ‌follows like the ‌wheel follows the ​ox.

### The Story ‌Where It Breaks ​(Savitri Cycle)

The ​Mahābhārata’s Savitrī tale ‌stages the doctrine’s limit-case: ‌Satyavān’s life exhausted ‌by karma’s count, ‌Yama arrives on ​schedule — and ‌the wife’s flawless ​speech wins the ​husband back. The ​epic never denies ‌the law; it shows ​a love so ​exact in its ​dharma that the ‌law’s own keeper ​must honour it.

### ​The Subtle Dust ​(Jain Mechanics)

Jainism ‌made karma physical: ​a subtle matter that ‌clings to the ​soul like dust ‌to a wet ​cloth, weighing it ‌into rebirth. The ‌doctrine’s imagery — ​the soul’s lightness ​restored by austerity ​until it rises like ​a flame released ‌— is the ‌most materialist eschatology ​India produced.
